newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 29.

text.p: THE DOMINION

A senior volcanologist involved in monitoring Mount Ruapehu is understood to be among high-profile scientific redundancies revealed on Monday. About 20 scientists are to be made redundant from the Geological and Nuclear Sciences crown research institute apparently because they are not money-spinners. Page 1.

ACT NZ has urged Labour to have its policies costed by the Treasury before committing to any coalition deal. ACT's finance spokesman Rodney Hide said on Monday no one knew whether Labour's economic policies were workable. Page 2.

Defeated longstanding Maori MP Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan has hit out at Ngai Tahu leaders, blaming their "plotting" as part of the reason she lost her seat in the election. In a speech in Christchurch on Monday, she suggested Ngai Tahu resources may have been used in a "subversive campaign" against her. Page 2.
ACT NZ's Wellington Central MP Richard Prebble has no immediate plans to fulfill his pre-election promise to move to Wellington. Page 2.
The Serious Fraud Office is conducting an inquiry into part of state-owned Airways Corporation, which runs New Zealand's air traffic control network. Page 3.

Lion Nathan is expect to report flat operating earnings when it issues its result on Thursday, mostly due to market share slippage in Australia. Forecasts for Lion's tax-paid net profit vary because of different estimates of its tax bill, but analysts generally expect a bottom-line figure of about $140 to $150 million, down from $202.3 million in the year to August 1995. Page 15.

ANZ Banking Group said on Monday it was not investigating or discussing a merger with London-based Standard Chartered Bank. Australian newspapers reported ANZ and Standard Chartered Bank were discussing plans for a A$24 billion (NZ$26.98 million) merger. Page 15.

Food group Goodman Fielder is confident profits will improve in the current financial year. "The market will remain tough but our success in strengthening the company gives me confidence that we will improve our results in the coming year and continue to build a very solid base for future growth," chairman David
Clarke said in the company's annual report.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

The Police Association is demanding that all frontline staff be armed with disabling pepper spray. It plans to meet police chiefs next week to discuss the issue and is confident that pepper spray will join the wooden baton as part of the police officer's standard arsenal.

The Clerk of Parliament, David McGee, says a significant proportion of law-making in New Zealand - relating to international agreements - is undemocratic. He says that the executive, the cabinet, is empowered to enter into international agreements without reference to Parliament. When it is referred back to Parliament for its blessing, it is a fait accompli.
The Otago University Students' Association has written to New Zealand First urging it to take account of "chronic underfunding" of universities when choosing a coalition partner.

A large tax provision is expected to significantly lower Lion Nathan's full-year August profit. Market forecasts of the brewer's profit, to be announced on Thursday, range from $147 million to $184.4 million.
Tradenz chief executive Rick Christie will become general manager international for the ANZ Bank after being head-hunted by the bank. He will take up his new post early next year.

Some advertising of investment opportunities in ostrich farming has been withdrawn after investigations by the Securities Commission, says the commission's chief executive John Farrell. However, he told potential investors the commission was "unable to give any priority" to investigating the industry.

The Canadian company which owns the Think Big methanol plants in Taranaki says their future depends on whether an economical substitute for Maui gas can be found. The 260 staff at Methanex Corporation's plant at Motonui and Waitara Valley
were briefed recently on options as Maui gas starts to run out. The giant gas field is due to run dry by 2005, three years earlier than expected.

As part of its merger with Westpac, Trust Bank has applied to the Reserve Bank for voluntary removal from the register of registered banks. This means it can no longer operate as a registered trading bank, but its owner Westpac can use the name Trust Bank as a brand.
